milestones.title: Disc extracted
milestones.detail: main.dol + 2.5 GB of game data pulled from the PAL disc (RM7P4F).

milestones.title: Executable split & analysed
milestones.detail: decomp-toolkit finds 12,580 functions in 707 objects; game code at 0x80006B40–0x80232AF8.

milestones.title: Tooling
milestones.detail: Cross-reference, renaming, progress, script-callback, name-hash and .sir decoding tools; this site updates on every push.

milestones.title: Boot path decompiled
milestones.detail: main(), SDK init, heaps, reset/power handling, crash screen, top-level game loop.

milestones.title: Engine & game systems
milestones.detail: Engine init/frame/shutdown, game startup, mode state machine and the renderer core (render thread, display lists, frame pacing) done; next: GX state, render targets, scene graph, UI, world, monsters, battles.

milestones.title: PC build compiles
milestones.detail: CMake + MSVC build on GitHub Actions, now 32-bit (Win32) so the decompiled code, which uses the original 4-byte pointer layout, is correct as written. All decompiled sources compile; x64 comes later, after named structs and a data loader.

milestones.title: PC build links
milestones.detail: The Windows build links into a real monsterlab.exe. Functions that are still missing get generated stubs that report their name and stop, and the stubs disappear as decompilation fills them in.

milestones.title: Big-endian data loader
milestones.detail: Convert game data from the Wii's big-endian format at load time. On PC now: the file catalog, all of global_binary.sir (database, input, textures, strings, script actions, UI, effects, screen sets), most of the front-end level (zones, entities, props, scene objects, pools, camera data), the shared zones and their screen sets with every widget kind, and the texture sections of shared_texture.sir. Everything is checked against the reference decoder.

milestones.title: Tested against the original
milestones.detail: Compare self-contained functions (math, part stats, opponent generation, loot rolls) with the original code on the same inputs.

milestones.title: SDK functions identified
milestones.detail: Apply RVL SDK / MSL / Bink signatures (decomp-toolkit, signatures from other RevoEX-2.1 decomps) to name more of the ~4,000 library functions, so the platform layer knows exactly which Nintendo SDK calls to replace.

milestones.title: Platform layer
milestones.detail: Windows replacements for the Wii system code: memory heaps, OS time, threads, reports, disc reads and the C library. The game's graphics commands run through a Direct3D 11 renderer, and the graphics state calls (blending, depth, texture combining and more) now send the same register values as on the Wii. Audio and input are still stubs.

milestones.title: Asset formats
milestones.detail: .sir containers (PNP0), DSP-ADPCM audio, Bink video, MIDI + wavetable music.

milestones.title: Boots to title screen
milestones.detail: The PC port now reaches the title screen from the player's own disc with Direct3D 11: the strap safety screen, the splash screens, then the Monster Lab logo and the press-A prompt. The 3D castle scene behind the logo still draws black; that renderer work comes next, together with real controller input.

milestones.title: 1080p & widescreen
milestones.detail: Renders at any resolution (--res, default 1920x1080) in 16:9 using the game's own widescreen mode, or 4:3; menus and logos keep their shape (or stretch like on a TV with an option). Done in PR #102.

milestones.title: Settings GUI
milestones.detail: In-game settings screen (F1 or Esc, Dear ImGui) saved to monsterlab.ini: resolution, aspect, stretched menus, V-sync, borderless fullscreen, frame-rate cap or uncapped, render scale, MSAA, texture filtering, volume, keyboard and gamepad rebinding, the game disc, plus an F3 stats overlay (PRs #104, #105, #111, #124, #129, #132, #133).

milestones.title: Own-disc setup (ISO picker)
milestones.detail: No game content is ever shipped. On first launch the player picks their own Monster Lab disc image (.iso) or extracted folder; the game is read straight from the image, checked to be the right game and region, and the choice is kept in monsterlab.ini, with a Game page in the settings to change it (PRs #107, #111). .wbfs and .rvz images are not supported yet.

milestones.title: Mod support
milestones.detail: Mods folder overriding any game file, plus new content in open formats: monster parts as glTF models, PNG textures and JSON/text stats, with no .sir editing needed.

milestones.title: Playable
milestones.detail: Full game playable from start to finish on PC.

milestones.title: 64-bit build
milestones.detail: After named structs and a loader replace raw offsets into game data. Not needed for 1080p, the settings GUI or mods.

changelog.text: Monster parts on the Monster Constructor are textured and shaded again instead of plain white: one light's direction was being read in the Wii's byte order, which made it an invalid number. Also a speed-up: calls to the game's tiniest functions no longer go through a slow CPU exception each time (about 150 a frame in the village), so the village frame drops from 23.0 to 20.2 ms.
Modding tool, step 3: a viewer for mod parts (.part files) that reloads by itself whenever the file changes, so part makers see their edits right away.
Modding tool, step 2b: a 3D view of the meshes in levels and in the shared monster parts, with an orbit camera, drawn the way the game draws them.
Modding tool, step 2a: a texture gallery and viewer for any .sir file, with export to PNG or DDS, plus the game's strings for mod makers.

First piece of the modding tool: a separate ml_modtool.exe that opens the game's .sir data files and shows their contents as a browsable tree, using the game's own loader so everything reads exactly as the game sees it. Texture and 3D model viewers follow next.
The story plays on past the Weld-O-Tron to the Lightning Tower without any new fixes needed; the playthrough test now covers 30 stages.

The Weld-O-Tron can be won: welds now register on the seam (its tiles' size data was being read in the Wii's byte order), the meter fills to 100, SUCCESS! appears and you return to the Mechanical Lab. The welded seam isn't drawn on screen yet. Also, the black hole head mod now looks like the reference: a black core with a thin, tilted, spinning disc of glowing amber gas, its light bending over the top and under the bottom, a bright ring at the edge, and a small projector on the neck.

Mods can now add brand-new monster parts and change the game's tables when it loads, without containing any game files. Modded parts keep a fixed number, recorded in a small file next to your saves, so turning a mod off or changing the mod order never mixes up your parts. The black hole head now uses this. Also, the last speed-up is in: vertices go straight to the graphics card, so drawing the village now takes 6.2 ms instead of 8.6 ms before the four performance steps, with an unchanged picture.

Black hole head mod, part 2: the game can now draw a brand-new head part from a mod (seen in a battle with a test switch), packed from the mod's own model and textures. It isn't in normal play yet; that waits for the save-safe part numbers. Its look is also still being reworked to match the reference: a tilted glowing disc with light bending over and under the black hole.

Drawing is about 1.2 ms cheaper per frame in the village and in battles: repeated draws that need no new setup now skip straight to adding their vertices, which is 95% of all draws. On an idle PC the village, battles and the castle all hold 60 fps at 1080p, and the picture is unchanged.

The Weld-O-Tron experiment is playable: its screen shows the seam, the welding gun, the meter and the heat gauge, the gun swings in, and holding B welds. If the gun overheats, the experiment fails and you return to the castle without a crash. Next: welding well enough to pass.

The first experiment, the Weld-O-Tron, now starts: its level loads, its screens appear and the two pages of instructions open (the arc welder and the seam's sparks were being read in the Wii's byte order). The button after the instructions still crashes; that's next. Also, the stutter when a level loads is about a third of what it was: compiled shaders are now kept on disk (the Command Room's worst frame went from about 120 ms to 40 ms).

Mods can now replace any game file, not just textures: each mod has a mod.ini with a name, on/off switch and priority, the F1 menu lists your mods, and the log says which files a mod replaced. A small sample mod is included. Also, the frame-time tools now measure the village, a battle and the castle reliably at any window size; the village currently takes 14.9 ms to draw out of a 23.9 ms frame, the starting point for the speed-ups.

Savestates in the game window: F5 saves, F8 loads and F6/F7 pick one of 10 slots, and the F1 menu has a Savestates page with a picture and time for each slot. A state from a different build of the game is refused with a message instead of crashing.

Two plans written: one for a steady frame rate at 1080p (measure properly, remove the stutter when a level loads, then cheaper drawing) and one for the 49 crashes in the function-comparison tests, grouped by cause, starting with a float-to-number conversion mistake in our own code.

Black hole head mod, part 1: a script now draws the new head's model, textures and part icons from scratch (a dark core with a glowing, swirling disc on a small projector), and notes how the game stores a part. The head isn't in the game yet; the next step adds it to the parts list.
Choosing ingredients for the first experiment works and leads into the Weld-O-Tron level; the playthrough test covers it (22 stages, PR #279).
The lab book (I.G.O.R.) finds its sections again, so your ingredients show up and the first experiment can be started; the game now plays on to the Weld-O-Tron experiment (PR #278).
Badges are no longer awarded at random: four award paths set the wrong badge on Windows. A playthrough now earns only Flyweight, at the first win, and every award is logged (PR #277).

Fixed a renderer bug that wrote past the end of a graphics buffer, a likely cause of the AMD driver crashes; every write into the graphics card's buffers is now bounds-checked, the soft-shadow pass uses valid settings, and --d3d-debug turns on Direct3D's checking mode (PR #276).

The game now plays further at the castle: after naming your scientist, Fuseless welcomes you, I.G.O.R. the lab book opens, and you walk through the Grand Hall into the Mechanical Lab to start your first experiment. The playthrough test covers it (21 stages, PR #275).
Cutscene movies play again when the game runs from the disc image (ISO, WBFS, RVZ) instead of an extracted folder (PR #274).

Savestates: tests can now start in the middle of the game (--save-state / --load-state, playthrough --from), and test runs repeat exactly (PR #270). New soft shadows option, on by default: the game's hard black shadows are blurred and see-through (PR #269). Texture packs: wider art for full-screen pictures fills a 16:9 screen (PR #272), and Dolphin texture packs with tex1_ names work (PR #273).

New lighting option, on by default: lit 3D scenes are no longer clipped to white, so the overexposed professor talk looks natural; the original look stays selectable in F1 (PR #268). The scientist name entry's letter keys now respond to the pointer (PR #271).

The settings screen (F1) has a Dump textures switch with a folder setting, so textures can be dumped at any moment (PR #266). Texture packs load in the background, so big packs no longer stall the game (PR #267).

Texture packs can use compressed DDS files (BC1/BC3/BC7 with mipmaps), and tools/png2dds.py converts a pack's PNGs (PR #264). The main menu rain is no longer saturated cyan: the renderer now uses the game's own smaller texture versions for distant drops (PR #265).
The Windows renderer no longer freezes forever if the graphics card fails to report back; it waits at most 2 seconds and logs what happened (PR #263).
Back at the castle, the screen where you name your scientist now opens instead of hanging (PR #262).

The game now plays further on Windows than we knew: a second battle against Belobog, the Combat Awards screen, the Mayor's thanks and the return to the castle all work. The playthrough test now checks all of it (16 stages, PR #261).
Differential tests now check 516 more functions against the original game; they fixed how opponents pick their parts and a few other small mistakes in our decompiled code (PR #260).
11 more places in our decompiled code now pass the values the original game passes instead of 0, and a new checker finds this kind of mistake automatically (PR #259).

A new automatic playthrough test plays from boot through the first battle and Field Repair to the free village map and reports how far it gets, so changes that break the game are caught before they are merged (PR #258).
The part you select in the battle now gets its highlight tint like on the Wii, and a few other calls in our decompiled code pass the values the original passes (PR #256).
Test runs without a window now draw in software, so they no longer load the graphics card next to a running game (PR #257).
777 more functions have names: game functions named after the part of the game they belong to, and the Bluetooth and online library code (PRs #252-#255).

Saving works on Windows: your profile is written to disk and Continue loads it back (PR #251). Differential tests found and fixed more small mistakes in our decompiled code (dropped arguments, a popup text, a rock check) (PR #250). About 290 more functions have names (PRs #225-#249).
The main menu's lightning bolts now branch and fork like on the Wii instead of looking wrong (PR #224).
Behind the scenes: our decompiled code's function declarations now all match their definitions, and the check tool catches mismatches like the one behind the Field Repair crash (PR #223).
Battle shows both monsters' real names, Gorbok and Mongor, instead of 'Not found' (PR #221). After Field Repair the game returns to the village map and you can walk on to the next spot (PR #222).
On the village map your monster now faces the way it walks (PR #219). The main menu's sky and sea move again, and so do other scrolling textures (PR #220).
In the Field Repair minigame the wheel now turns when you swing and the round ends (PR #217).
The game's pointing hand no longer shrinks after switching cursors, and a new setting shows the Windows mouse cursor over the game for anyone who wants it (PR #218).
The first battle now plays to the end on Windows (PR #216): you win, see the results and the reward, return to the village, and the Field Repair minigame starts.
The Windows mouse cursor no longer shows over the game, and the game's pointing hand is drawn at its true 64x64 size at every resolution (PR #215).

The village intro's coffin now falls at the Wii's speed and its model is drawn (PRs #211, #214): game objects were being updated twice per frame. The village holds 60 fps in our test runs (PR #213). Renamed functions no longer break the build (PR #210).

On the village map the camera follows your monster and pans to the enemies after the Mayor, matching the Wii (checked in PR #207, which also adds frame-sequence screenshots for tests). 17 more functions have names (PRs #208, #209).

All 3D drawing now runs on the graphics card, so scenes cost less per frame (PRs #205). Differential tests now cover more of the battle and camera code and caught 4 small mistakes in our decompiled code (PR #200). About 540 more functions have names, by exact behaviour or by their simple shape (PRs #196-#204).

Battle attack and hit sounds now play: they were triggered by the animation events fixed in PR #189. A new sound log (PR #191) shows every sound the game asks for and whether it played. 89 more functions have real names (PRs #192, #193, #195).
In the first battle the enemy now faces your monster, and the attack camera moves and animation events play (PR #189).

The first battle now plays on Windows (PR #187): attacks play out, the enemy takes its turn, and the fight runs for two rounds. The 3D scenes are now drawn on the graphics card, so the village takes about 40% less work per frame (PR #188).

The first battle now loads and starts on Windows (PR #183): the arena, the intro camera, the combat tutorial and choosing a part with the stick. Cutscene movies no longer show thin vertical lines at other window sizes (PR #186).
After the village fly-over the camera now cuts to the normal map view while the coffin falls, as on the Wii (PR #184). Rendering the village takes a little less work per frame (PR #185).

Your monster appears on the village map on Windows (PR #180): it stands on the map spot and walks to the next one. The level's table of monster parts was still in the Wii's byte order, so the game couldn't build the monster.

New F12 capture key on Windows (PR #179): it saves the decoded movie frame, the game's internal picture and the final window picture, plus the current settings, into a captures folder next to the game. It's for tracking down picture problems that only show on some setups.

The first battle triggers on Windows (PR #178): walking to the monsters blocking the village path now starts the battle, and the arena level begins loading. It stays on the loading screen for now; that's next.

Faster rendering on Windows (PR #177): the screen copies the game makes for its effects now reuse a pool of textures instead of creating new ones, which cut the time spent on copies on the main menu from 24 seconds to 0.4 seconds over a 3,900-frame test run.

More of the game converted (PRs 175 176): the whole character definition is now converted to PC byte order, not just the animation speed (#175); and the village map camera no longer goes wrong after a conversation, because the player's camera sensor radius was unconverted and every camera zone applied at once (#176).

Thunder rolls on the main menu (PR #174): a thunder clap every 3 to 5 seconds, as in the real game. The timed triggers that play it were converted without their actions and time-outs, so they never fired.

Characters animate in the game on Windows (PR #173): Professor Fuseless and the other characters stood still because the animation speed in their definitions was still in the Wii's byte order, which made every animation step almost zero. Now they move. More of the character definitions still needs converting.

Lightning flashes on the main menu again (PR #172): the lightning's timer handler got its arguments in the wrong order on PC, so the frame time was lost and the bolts never came back after the first one. The thunder sound is next. The F3 overlay now shows both the game's frame rate and how many pictures are shown per second (PR #171).

Fixed the game stopping on the main menu after a while (PR #170). When the Wii Remote's rumble timer fired, our decompiled handler didn't receive its timer, and the function it needed wasn't in the PC version yet. Both are fixed, checked against the original game code.

Further into the game on Windows (PR #169): after the village intro, the exploration map works, and walking to the next spot opens the conversation with Mayor Neidervoten. Also, the faint ghost image over the main menu is gone (PR #168). The game's glow effect makes half-size copies of the screen, and the PC version had been making them full size, so an old picture showed through.

Mods can now change the game's text (PR #166): a JSON file in a mod overrides entries of the game's text table, checked when it loads, and --dump-data exports the original table from your own disc to start from. Also, arrow keys and the D-pad now work on the Options screen (PR #167); its sliders, rumble, volume and saving were checked and already worked.

Big step on Windows (PRs #161 to #165). The village intro cutscene finishes: the coffin lands and the exploration map shows. The main menu now has its rain and the projector's light cone with the menu text inside. The sound mixer now has the game's reverb, echo, chorus and delay effects, and the Wii Remote speaker's sounds play through your PC speakers, with a setting to turn that off. Mods can now replace textures by their name in the game's data instead of a hash.

Continue on the main menu now loads your saved game on Windows (PR #159), and selecting a profile works. The differential tests now report every small self-contained function as matching the original Wii code, apart from 18 listed cases the test harness can't run yet. That came with one more fix in our decompiled code (PR #158).

Every cutscene on the disc now decodes correctly on Windows (PR #154): all 78 movies, with picture and all five audio tracks, sound within 0.04 s of the picture. Skipping a cutscene with a button is now tested too (PR #157). In the village intro the coffin's template is now found, because a name lookup table is converted to PC byte order (PR #156); the cutscene still waits at the same picture for now. And more differential-test fixes in our decompiled code (PR #155).

Further into the game on Windows (PR #153, which includes #152). The opening conversation with Professor Fuseless plays, with voice lines, and advances with A, and the village map level loads and its intro cutscene starts. The cutscene doesn't finish yet: the coffin never lands. On the main menu, the projector machine now draws (PR #151), and the mouse cursor now stays under the mouse at the top and bottom of the screen (PR #148).
Cutscenes play on Windows (PR #150): the game's Bink movies now show with picture and sound, starting with the intro movie, through the game's own drawing code. --no-movies skips them.

Characters in the first level now come to life (PR #149). Professor Fuseless and the other characters were never woken up, because their wake-up events weren't converted to PC byte order. And the graphics command buffer never rolled over when full, so drawing an animated character overwrote nearby memory. The Command Room now runs up to the professor's first voice line. Also new: a Bink video decoder for the game's cutscenes, built from FFmpeg's open-source decoder (LGPL) and matching it exactly on the intro movie; it gets hooked into the game next (PR #147). And more differential-test fixes: bit shifts, the Lab inventory layout and how monster parts are copied (PR #146).

The differential tests found their first real mistakes (PR #144): 7 decompiled functions gave different results from the original Wii code, among them float range checks the wrong way round, a wrong constant and a wrong return value. All 7 now match the original.

A new game's story starts on Windows (PR #140): after Join Now!, the arrival event plays and the conversation with Professor Fuseless opens. It stops a few frames later for now. The quest's state data and voice lines are now converted to PC byte order. New differential tests (PR #143): tools/difftest.py runs each function's original Wii code next to our C++ on the same inputs and compares the results. Of 5,523 functions tested so far, 5,364 match exactly; the rest are being checked. Also, 175 mid-size functions were checked against the original by hand and had no mistakes (PR #141).

The projector machine on the main menu now wakes up (PR #139): its data, animations, size and angles are converted to PC byte order, and objects in general now get their real size instead of almost zero. It doesn't show on screen yet; finding where it's drawn is next.

Mod support for the Windows version (PR #138, which includes the work of #135 and #137). Put a mod in mods/<name>/ next to the game to replace any file from the disc. PNG images can replace game textures, and --dump-textures exports the originals from your own disc to start from. The settings screen has a Mods page to turn mods on and off and set their order. docs/modding.md has a worked example. Separately, 4 more mistakes in our decompiled code were fixed after checking the remaining game functions against the original (PR #136).
New settings on Windows (PRs #132, #133): MSAA anti-aliasing at 2x, 4x or 8x, and gamepad buttons can now be rebound in the controls page.

Frame-rate settings on Windows (PR #129): a frame-rate cap, your display's own rate, or uncapped, in the settings screen and monsterlab.ini. The game logic keeps its normal speed; only drawing goes faster.

Checked about 165 larger engine functions (rendering, effects, animation, the UI engine, sound) against the original game code and fixed 5 mistakes in our decompiled code (PR #131). Audited functions are listed in docs/audit_log.txt.

More of the PC version works (PRs #123, #124, #125, #130). On the main menu, pointing at Options and pressing A opens the Options screen. The game can also read .wbfs disc images, and the settings screen has render scale (50 to 200%) and texture filtering (nearest, bilinear or anisotropic). Two mistakes in our decompiled code were fixed: the scan reticle wrote three numbers into room for two, and a badge notice used the wrong queue index. The first level now runs for about 1,250 frames.

The first level loads and draws on Windows (PR #128): after Join Now! on the main menu, castle_communication now loads instead of crashing. Attach points, the aim object, scene lights and one more material type are converted to PC byte order. The main menu's camera also flies in to the wide shot of the castle, as on the Wii, now that animation entries are converted (PR #127). And the game can read .rvz disc images, Dolphin's compressed format (PR #126).

The main-menu camera now follows the level's own camera path (PR #122): three data-conversion errors kept it fixed in place. It isn't yet the wide shot of the castle you see on the Wii. The Options screen's sliders are now fully converted too (PR #121), a step towards opening Options from the menu.

Join Now! works on Windows (PR #120): choosing it on the main menu starts a new game, leaves the front end and starts loading the first level, castle_communication. Getting there took several fixes: game sounds and their audio headers are now converted to PC byte order, the level's lighting and object flags too, and a wait for the audio interrupt no longer hangs the game. The level crashes while loading for now, on a prop's bone data that still needs converting. That's next.

Hovering the mouse over a main-menu item now highlights it as on the Wii: brighter and larger, with a backing plate (PR #119). Clicking and arrow keys don't work yet. Also, --to-menu in a window now shows its progress in the title bar and keeps the window painted while it skips ahead (PR #117).

The main menu runs about three times faster on Windows (PR #118): from about 14 to about 44 frames per second at 1080p. The renderer now groups draws together and cuts the overhead of each of the roughly 2,250 draws per frame. The next step is moving the vertex work to the graphics card.

Two fixes towards a living main-menu scene (PR #116). Level objects were updated with a frame time of 0, so their animations never advanced; now animated props and particle emitters move. And the game's clock read its two halves the wrong way round, giving an absurd time value. The castle scene itself is still mostly static: its camera doesn't move yet, and most of its objects aren't active. That's next.

New smoke test, tools/smoke.py (PR #114): in under a minute it builds, runs the self-test and boots to the title and the main menu headless, then checks nothing crashed or came out blank. Every session now runs it before opening a PR. Also, the build script works again after two changes clashed (PR #115), and with the whole game optimised the game logic runs about 60% faster (about 150 instead of 93 frames per second, measured without drawing).

The whole Windows version is now built with compiler optimisation (PR #113), not just the PC parts. Some auto-generated functions returned small values whose top bits the callers then read, which only went wrong once optimised; they now return full values. Also, --to-menu in a window reaches the main menu in about 28 seconds instead of two minutes, because it skips drawing while fast-forwarding (PR #112).

Choose your own game disc (PR #111): on first start, the Windows version shows a screen where you pick your Monster Lab disc image or extracted folder. It checks that it's the right game and remembers the choice in monsterlab.ini; the settings screen has a Game page to change it. Also, the window now shows fast-forward progress while --to-menu skips the intro (PR #110). At 1080p that skip takes a couple of minutes in a window, so it isn't stuck.

Faster testing on Windows (PR #108): --to-menu fast-forwards past the intro to the main menu (about 23 seconds headless instead of over a minute), --fast-forward N skips ahead N frames, and rebuilds only recompile changed files, 0.3 to 3.5 seconds instead of 15. The game's clock is now virtual, so a fast-forwarded run reaches the same screens. Also fixed one place where our decompiled code broke with compiler optimisation: three callers gave a function room for two numbers where it writes three (PR #109).

The Windows version can now read the game straight from your own Monster Lab disc image (PR #107): start it with --iso followed by the path to your .iso. There's no need to extract the disc first; files are decrypted as they're read. The disc-picking screen comes next.

New test option for the Windows version (PR #106): --pointer X,Y@FRAME moves the Wii Remote pointer from a script, and the menu's cursor hand follows it. It's a first step towards selecting main-menu items with the mouse, which doesn't work yet; the menu is also still off-centre.

Settings screen on Windows (PR #105): press F1 or Esc for display settings (resolution, 16:9 or 4:3, stretched menus, vsync, borderless fullscreen, stats overlay), volume and mute, and key rebinding: click a control, then press the new key. Settings are saved to monsterlab.ini next to the game. While the screen is open, the game doesn't get your keys or mouse.

Stats overlay on Windows (PR #104): press F3, or start with --stats, for a panel in the top-right corner. It shows frames per second, frame time and its split into game, rendering and waiting, draw calls, effect copies, textures and audio voices. It's built with the open-source Dear ImGui library, which the settings screen will use next.

Fades and animations now play on Windows (PR #103). Three of our decompiled functions passed 0 instead of the frame time, so every fade and tween using them stood still. Now the splash screens fade, the logo glows and its arcs animate, and the game cycles from the splash screens to the title and the castle fly-by as on the Wii. Fog is now drawn too. The castle behind the title logo is still hidden by a black picture.

The Windows version renders at 1080p in widescreen (PR #102). The 3D scene uses the game's own 16:9 mode, and the menus and logos keep their shape instead of being stretched like on a TV. Other resolutions and 4:3 are options. The frame-buffer copies used for glow effects no longer create a new texture each time, which makes it faster.

The main menu draws on Windows (PR #101): after pressing A at the title, Join Now!, Continue, Select Profile, Options and Credits appear over the 3D castle scene. The menu's text was missing because the game's font tables were still in the Wii's byte order. Also, 73 more game functions have their real names, taken from the game's own debug messages (PR #100).

Checked 149 larger in-level gameplay functions (world, characters, camera, waypoints, triggers) against the original game code and fixed 5 mistakes in our decompiled code (PR #98). Two world-state flags were written as whole words, overwriting the bytes next to them. The player respawn call was missing an argument. A particle spawn copied one word too many, and an entity colour loop read its count from the wrong place.

The Windows version runs faster (PR #99): the PC parts (graphics, sound mixer and data loader) are now built with compiler optimisation, which takes the boot from about 34 to about 46 frames per second against the Wii's 50. The decompiled game code still builds unoptimised for now, because optimising it makes the game crash at the start. Finding the functions behind that is next.

494 more Wii SDK and library functions have their real names (PR #95), matched against the public, free-to-reuse Mario Kart Wii and Twilight Princess decomps. About 1,100 library functions are now named, including much of the online, HOME-menu and C-runtime code.

Sound works on Windows (PR #97): the title music plays. The PC version now mixes the game's own sound channels itself and plays them through Windows, with the Wii's compressed audio decoded and looped as on the console. Our decompiled music code also asked for one file where the disc has separate left and right tracks; that's fixed too. Echo effects and the Wii Remote's speaker aren't done yet. Separately, all 118 larger battle functions were checked against the original game code, and 7 mistakes in our decompiled battle code were fixed (PR #96).

Fixed five functions that were declared differently in different files (PR #94). Each one now matches the original game code, so the PC version passes them the right arguments. The prototype check now reports no conflicts.

You can control the game on Windows now (PR #93). Keyboard, mouse and Xbox-style gamepads stand in for the Wii Remote and Nunchuk, with the mouse as the pointer. Pressing A on the title screen plays its exit animation and opens the main menu. The menu's own pictures don't draw yet. The controls are kept in one table, ready for the settings screen later.

484 more Wii SDK and library functions have their real names (PR #92), up from 77. A new tool, tools/sig_match.py, compares the game's code against the public, free-to-reuse ogws project, which rebuilds the same Nintendo libraries. Every exact match gets its real name, across the system, graphics, audio, Wii Remote and Bluetooth code and the C runtime. Now it's clear exactly which library calls the PC version has to provide.

Checked all 289 larger menu, save and Lab functions against the original game code and fixed 10 mistakes in our decompiled code (PR #91). Among them, unlocked parts now get the right tier and quality, quest rewards show the right value, the matchup screen reads the waiting-opponent flag correctly, and a menu animation runs at the right speed. A log of every checked function is in docs/audit_log.txt.
17 more Wii SDK functions have their real names (PR #90): system clock and threads, video timing, the audio DSP, and graphics setup. That's 77 named so far.

The title screen shows on Windows! (PRs #86 to #89) The Monster Lab logo appears with its orange letters, the eye, the green LAB tube and the glowing light bulb, plus the 'press A' prompt. The PC version now acts as if a Wii Remote with a Nunchuk is plugged in, so the game no longer covers everything with its 'reconnect the controller' message. Title-screen pictures are now read in the Wii's byte order, the screen's glow layer covers its full width, and each level's fog and lighting settings are converted. The background scene behind the logo is still black.

Started naming the Nintendo Wii SDK and library code inside the game (PRs #83, #84, #85). A new map in docs/sdk_libraries.md shows where each library sits: the Wii system libraries, online play, the C runtime, Bink video and the debugger. 60 functions got their real names, including the audio, Wii Remote, graphics texture and disc functions. This shows exactly what the PC version has to provide in their place.

Fixed the 13 functions that broke the castle view on Windows (PR #82). They were set up to return a number they never actually return, so the PC's maths stack filled up. With the fix, the castle level's camera stays valid and the game reaches its title state without crashing. The title screen itself doesn't draw yet: that's renderer work.

Found why the castle view broke on Windows (PR #81): some of our generated functions leave a stray number on the PC processor's maths stack, and once eight pile up every calculation comes out as 'not a number'. Added a check that catches the leak and a tool that lists the 13 functions causing it. Fixing them comes next.

More of each level object's drawing settings are now read in the Wii's byte order (PR #80), including the brightness value the castle models were getting wrong. The castle still draws black on Windows, so the colour work continues.

It confirmed how global_binary.sir boots: a 4 KB pointer table plus a memory image that must load at 0x90400000, holding e.g. the "HOME Menu not available" icon and the fallback "Generic_box" model. Name lookup now also scans the large archives (shared_ui.sir etc.).

Decompiled the Wii Remote shake mini-games: catching a pumpkin (10 shakes within 5 seconds), clearing obstacles (fill a meter to 10) and powering generators (meter to 6), both draining at 3 units per second, plus combat start when an enemy gets close to the player.

Decompiled the first AI state callbacks under their original names (PatrolIdleEntry, PumpkinWait/Freeze/Escape/Death, HazardPoisonGas/DustCloud, MovingChallengeGame...) and their registration table. Added a hash resolver: object and UI ids in the code are CRC-32 hashes of names, and 390 of them now resolve (e.g. "Projectile", "exploration_screen", "timer_group").

Recovered about 2,000 original function names from the game's script-callback tables (e.g. PumpkinShakeUpdate, DiggingPlayThrustAnim, PuzzleMovePiece, InterpolateQuaternionTask::Update_SLERP). Named game functions jumped from 240 to 2,257, and about 20 earlier guessed names were corrected to the real ones.

Decompiled the play-session block: restoring saved object states into a zone, temporarily disabled objects that re-enable on a timer, the session timer, and the moving-character registry (max 20 per level, tracking the player and enemy indices).

Decompiled the core game-state block (reset, two-player turn timers with a 6-second hand-over, world update, camera follow reset) and the build info: this disc is EU build 519 from Aug 28 2008 (14:30).

Decompiled the save system: Wii NAND save file game.msa, save banner and icon setup (the banner defaults still name the engine's previous game, Death Jr. 2), read/write with NAND error codes, and the loading picture shown while saving.

Decompiled the disc-error screens (no disc / wrong disc / unreadable, with reset and power handling while they are shown), helper-entity spawning and target-lead prediction. Lab notes now show the time of each entry.

Decompiled the UI glue (screen manager, per-zone screen sets from ui/ScreenSets/ScreenSets.csv), the full mode-transition logic, the loading screen, language selection (EN/FR/DE/IT/ES/NL from the Wii system language), the movie queue, background-music requests and the 3D audio listener. 116 game functions decompiled.

Decompiled the renderer core: a dedicated render thread with a 64-entry command queue, a ring of 17 display-list buffers (144 KB each) recorded by redirecting the GX FIFO, frame-buffer flips and frame pacing on TV retrace, plus RendInit. This is the layer the PC port will replace with a modern GPU backend for 1080p and widescreen.

Decompiled the top-level game-mode state machine (GameUpdate), including in-game Bink movie playback from fmv/ and fmv_PAL/. Added memory/core init, suspend/resume, view objects and game shutdown. Windows build now runs on GitHub Actions (MSVC).

Decompiled the engine lifecycle (EngineInit, EngineFrame, memory callbacks for the REND and SG modules) and game startup (GameInit, GameStart, which loads global_binary.sir). Planned 1080p, a settings GUI and mod support.
